title: Improvisation: soloists, solo length and cueing
summary: Johnston asks how Gil inspires soloists. He explains solo lengths, needling from the piano and why he lets players stretch.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you, move at least move at this point really to some definitive things about your own music. Now you are a contemporary composer and you deal certainly with improvisations. (LAUGHTER). As anybody who has heard your music knows very well. How do you motivate or provoke or whatever word you might want to use and how do you inspire which I think is even a more important word, the particular performer to do what you really want him to do? Can you account for it in any way? I know this is a kind of difficult question.
The question isn't hard to answer but it's hard to answer it in a general way, but specifically......
Well treat it anyway you want to.
You could name me something that you have in mind or play name me something that I could tell you, but to tell you without hearing what you mean
I don't really know whether I could do that or not.

Oh, well I heard you live recently at Henry Street and your saxophonist there and your trumpet player too, both of them had extended solos so would you take them as cases in point? Then we can go to some of the recordings.

The funny part of it is, in that concert I couldn't hear them at all where I was sitting. And I decided that that was the last concert I'll ever play without having a monitor speaker on the stage, you know. For me and one for the drummer so that we can hear everybody because it's, certain currents go certain ways and if you're caught in the crossfire, sometimes you can't hear certain people.

And I could not hear the soloists at all in that job. And I heard them when I came home on a little bit of tape that Anita made from a video tape because the machine wasn't working, a battery or something, but the man down there who hired me, Chuck Fowler, tape recorded it so I'll be able to hear it.
But anyway, we were talking about the improvisation and your own kind of inspiration or way of inspiring people or way of provoking them to get what

you want. Speaking specifically at this point about your trumpet player and your saxophone player, Billy Harper, at the most recent concert that I heard you give. But this brings you to anything you want to about improvisation......

The length of their solos is really determined by them. Sometimes we write down a definite number of choruses an tunes. 2. It seems like a lot of them so it's extended, but it may have a definite end to it, on the parts, because it's a possibility.
Sometimes they (?) a tune and they don't want to play any more and then we go on from there.
Well what happens when you find that what they are doing becomes repetitive? Do you have a way of poking in or do you still wait them out?

Well you can needle them a little bit you know. I can needle them at the piano or the drums can change sometimes if it does seem that it's getting too, if the groove is becoming a rut. Then you can do that. Sometimes you do it that way or....... You try to create something that will possible lead them a different way, a different direction. You can do that.
Or you could have an ensemble available that you just cue the band in, they come in and take it out.
But in any case, you do make some judgement about ......
